messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] naming prob and cdf functions?
messages.body_plain:
On 8/31/12 5:49 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
> On Fri, Aug 31, 2012 at 5:12 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>> 1.  I agree that random_normal is better than rand_normal.
>
> Thinking about it more, I would also propose normal_random to be
> consistent with normal_log, normal_cdf etc.

Yup.  That makes sense to me.

How do people feel about normal_cdf() vs. normal_p()?

Again, at this point, renaming is a pain, as we'd
want to add normal_cdf() and deprecate normal_p().

>> 2.  Earlier, I'd liked the idea that y ~ normal (0,1) in the generated quantities block gets translated into y <- random_normal (0,1).
>>
>> But now I have mixed feelings.  Now that I fully understand that "~" maps directly into a log-probability statement, I'm not so happy about overloading the "~" symbol so that it means different things in different blocks of the program.
>>
>> One difficulty I think we're _always_ going to have with users (including me) is confusion between ~ and <-.  Back when I wrote Bugs code, I was always typing <- for ~ or vice-versa.

Odd.  That's one confusion I never had.  But then
I'm a programming language type freak and I knew
how these operations were implemented in updates.

My problem is that I keep trying to use the equal
sign for assignment everywhere.  The use of <- seems
restricted to R and its syntactic descendants,
BUGS, JAGS, and now Stan.

>> I have the impression that for a stan model, that any expression can be ~ or <- but not both.  That is, depending on declarations, if the statement
>> foo1 <- foo2
>> is correct, then
>> foo1 ~ foo2
>> is incorrect.

There's nowhere at the moment that both of those
would be legal, because the right side of ~ needs to be
a distribution name and parameters and the
right side of <- needs to be a general expression.

x ~ foo(a,b,c);   ===>   lp__ += foo_log(x,a,b,c);

x <- foo(a,b,c);  ===>    x = foo(a,b,c);

There is no foo such that both foo_log() and foo() is
a function, so there's no foo where both are well defined.

> And vice-versa.  So in fact the choice of "~" or "<-" is in fact a piece of redundant information.
 > That's ok, a bit of redundancy is ok.  In any case, I'm pretty sure that when
 > I write Stan models I will continue to use ~ instead of <- and vice-versa.  It's just hard to keep straight.
>
> In the model block
>
> foo1 <- foo2(a,b)
>
> is not the same as
>
> foo1 ~ foo2(a,b)
>
> The first means assignment of a value (i.e., in C++ foo1 = foo2(a,b);)
> while the second declares something as being distributed according to
> a distribution.  The second gets translated into:
>
> lp__ += foo2_log(foo1,a,b);
>
> I prefer overloading ~ because it has an intuitive match to a commonly
> used notation.  In the generated quantities block the second statement
> would become something like:
>
> random_normal(foo1,a,b);
>
> Note that this does imply a restricted statement syntax for the LHS of
> a ~ in the generated quantities block.

Good point.  The a in a ~ will need to be assignable (aka an lvalue).

I can just test that the a is assignable (aka an lvalue) by
attaching a semantic action to the rule that only fires in

the generated quantities block.

> I suppose that's the one
> advantage of using <- in generated quantities because that rule would
> be consistent.

It would certainly be easier.

But then you get an inconsistency that you have a function
random_normal() that can only be applied in the generated
quantities block.

A halfway approach would be to treat normal(mu,sigma) as a function
that returns a normal variate.  So you could have

     y_rep <- normal(mu,sigma);

in the generated quantities block.  But then we're back to
functions that only exist in one block.

Recall that we decided to not go with random functions in the data block.
It would seriously complicate the design, because up until now,
the data gets assigned once and reused for multiple chains.  If that
were the interpretation we wanted, it'd be easy enough.  But there's
really no good way to output variables from the transformed data block
anyway.

It might be possible to use some randomization inside other
loops in the tansformed params or params, but then it would
get executed once per leapfrog step.

But the more I think about it, the more I like just overloading
with a side test that the LHS is an lvalue.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On 8/31/12 5:25 PM, Nigel/essence wrote:
> Thanks - there seems to be some good discussion arising. I am based in UK, so will not attempt to respond much this evening.

> I am pretty familiar with NUTS, having converted it from Matlab to Java (not trivial with the recursion!).
>
> The jiggling of epsilon I am referring to is in lines 156-161 of nuts.hpp, and if I understand it, the jiggling
 > only happens AFTER burn in, which is what I was wondering about.
 > Have I understood correctly, and is there a reason for this?
 > It seems strange - I definitely want to jiggle during burn in, otherwise I will never get out of burn in.

I seem to recall discussing this with Matt when I put
in the parameter that adjusted the step size epsilon
+/- some percentage around the adapted size.

I believe the conclusion was that we thought it might
confuse the adaptation, which was already working well.

Matt didn't think moving epsilon was going to help,
but since then, we've run into some more complicated
geometries where moving it way down every few iterations
seems like it might help.

> The papers on DREAM are well worth the effort, and Gregory has
> found it very useful for his work finding aliens. Look up Gregory and FUSION,
 > he is from Toronto, and has similar background to me (I also did theoretical physics PhD at Manchester).

I found this:  http://www.phas.ubc.ca/~gregory/gregory.html

He seems to be one emeritus professor who's still going
gangbusters, which I think is fantastic (because that's where
I want to be some day).

I'll see if I can get through the papers.  These have been
more in Matt Hoffman's and Michael Betancourt's domain
(Michael's also a theoretical physicist);  with their
help in front of a blackboard, I can almost feel like I'm
getting the easier parts.

What is always amazing to me is that after the dust
settles, the algorithms are usually pretty straightforward.
(NUTS is involved, but I'm a computer scientist, so recursive
binary tree algorithms are comfort food.)

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On 8/31/12 5:12 PM, Matt Hoffman wrote:
> ... I'm not very

> familiar with DE, but it's probably worth looking into. My
> understanding is that it generates proposals roughly in the direction
> of the vectors between points in parallel chains, an idea that's quite
> closely related to Zhang and Sutton's BFGS HMC algorithm.

 > ... But it's nice that they satisfy detailed balance and

> don't require O(N^2) computation/storage.

On a related note, I'm hoping to add Goodman and Weare's
sampler to Stan soon.
of Goodman and Weare's sampler, which
   http://msp.org/camcos/2010/5-1/p04.xhtml

It samples on the ray connecting a pair of samples on
parallel chains.  It does have O(N^2) memory and update
cost where N is the number of parameters, because the current points
on each chain need to span the parameter space and all need
to be updated each iteration.  So thousands
of parameters will probably be a practical max on current hardware.
On the plus side, it's  rotation and scale invariant,
doesn't require gradients, is very easy to parallelize,
and generates N parallel chains.

I still don't quite understand the convergence evaluation or
the effective sample size calcs in this situation, though.
There's some discussion in their paper, but I don't see how
it deals with the fact that you have correlations across chains.

Matt and Michael B. weren't too enthusiastic when I explained how
it worked, but I can't recall their concerns.  But it's so
simple to implement and new samplers are so easy to integrate
into Stan (which exposes log prob and gradient functions with
unconstraining transforms built in) that I can add it and evaluate
all the BUGS models pretty easily.

- Bob

library(rstan)

$env
$env$PKG_LIBS
[1] " -L/usr/lib/R/site-library/Rcpp/lib -lRcpp -Wl,-rpath,/usr/lib/R/site-library/Rcpp/lib"

$includes
[1] "\n#include <Rcpp.h>\n\n\n#ifndef BEGIN_RCPP\n#define BEGIN_RCPP\n#endif\n\n#ifndef END_RCPP\n#define END_RCPP\n#endif\n\nusing namespace Rcpp;\n"

$LinkingTo
[1] "Rcpp"

$body
function (x)
{
    sprintf("BEGIN_RCPP\n%s\nEND_RCPP", x)
}
<environment: 0x7f8010bdd278>

$Depends
[1] "Rcpp"

$Makevars
 [1] "## Use the R_HOME indirection to support installations of multiple R version"
 [2] "PKG_LIBS = `$(R_HOME)/bin/Rscript -e \"Rcpp:::LdFlags()\"`"
 [3] ""
 [4] "## As an alternative, one can also add this code in a file 'configure'"

But only some flags can be set.  The truth is those PKG_CXXFLAGS are inserted into ALL_CXXFLAGS, which is really used for compiling the source code.  So whatever you do in PKG_CXXFLAGS for the optimization level would be overwritten by what is in CXXFLAGS in R.home('etc')/Makeconf or the Makeconf in the home directory.  But if there is no -g in CXXFLAGS, we might be able to add one if that helps.

Jiqiang

messages.subject: Rosenbrock test function with NUTS
messages.body_plain:
Has anybody tried NUTS with standard optimisation test functions such as Rosenbrock?

I am doing some tests, using these functions as the negative log likelihood.

Preliminary tests, with N = 16, and without any mass weight, shows that DE methods are vastly superior to NUTS, and indeed random walk is better than NUTS, but this is expected to change as soon as I implement the exact Hessian weights in NUTS.

My evaluation is very simplistic - whether the sampler gets anywhere near the minimum in a few million function/gradient evals.

As a cross check against my Java code, I will also try the original Matlab NUTS code on this example.

I'm not sure whether there are analytical integations for these functions, against which MCMC sampled cdf's can be compared.

I guess my question is - how many test functions has NUTS been evaluated against? In the optimisation, world, there is a standard set of test problems, but I haven't seen a similar set for MCMC methods - might be a useful exercise to generate a standard set so the community can properly evaluate different approaches.

Not very exciting work, but extremely valuable, and IMHO a necessary condition for a mature technology.

I will shortly test NUTS with the exact Rosenbrock Hessian and report back, and then some time soon try some BFGS methods for comparison.

I also need to examine whether my actual problem has an analytical Hessian - it probably does, but has some lengthy algebra to evaluate, and I am sure it is not positive definite everywhere - but maybe I can see a reasonable analytic approximation which is.

messages.subject: Re: Rosenbrock test function with NUTS
messages.body_plain:
On Sunday, September 2, 2012 9:02:47 AM UTC-4, Nigel/essence wrote:
> Has anybody tried NUTS with standard optimisation test functions such as Rosenbrock?
>
> I am doing some tests, using these functions as the negative log likelihood.

Stan includes many tests, although not this one. One difficulty with subjecting Stan (or any NUTS algorithm) to some difficult minimization problem is that you have to ensure that the "posterior" is a proper distribution. In many situations, the objective function would not integrate to a finite number in the typical case where each parameter can take any value on the real line. So, I would think that a necessary condition for such a test is that you would have to bound the parameters to [-100,100] or some other wide interval that includes the optimum.

The original plan for Stan was to include support for optimization using automatic differentiation to obtain the gradient and / or Hessian in situations where one or both is not easy to calculate analytically. Indeed, optimization is mentioned in TO-DO.txt. I don't know that optimization algorithms are a top priority for any of us at the moment, but if someone else wanted to push forward with them, great. Although I would think we should start with a design for an optimization module and then implement the textbook optimization algorithms that wouldn't work well Rosenbrock's function.

Ben

messages.subject: DREAM: Rosenbrock! ESS? tuning?
messages.body_plain:
Speaking of Rosenbrock, I'm going to implement
Vrugt et al.'s DREAM:

   http://jasper.eng.uci.edu/pdf/47.pdf

It should handle the Rosenbrock reasonably well.
It's a multi-point method that's related to
Nelder-Mead optimization (an analogy brought up
by Goodman and Weare in their ensemble sampling
paper, which is very very closely related
to DREAM's precursor, which the above paper
calls DE-MC).

The DREAM algorithm's very straightforward
and it doesn't require gradients.  It will
require

   - templating the log prob function in the
     model for efficiency, and

   - coming up with a multi_sampler and
     adaptive_multi_sampler interface.

I'm thinking something simple for the latter folloiwng
adaptive_sampler, but with a method signature

   void multi_sample(vector<double>& thetas);

I could probably drop the "multi_" as it's implicit
in the argument.

Speaking of muti-point samplers, does anyone know how
to deal with ESS calcs for something like DREAM
where the different chains are correlated?  There's
some discussion in Goodman and Weare's paper:

http://msp.berkeley.edu/camcos/2010/5-1/camcos-v5-n1-p04-p.pdf

Also, does anyone know if there's something I should
read about implementation or parameters, or are
the defaults in that paper still standard operating
procedure?

- Bob

I'm not surprised.  I responsed about DREAM and its
predecessor DE.  In short, we can add DREAM to Stan.

Stan's basic modeling and sampling framework was intended
to be flexible enough to let us play with different
samplers.  We started with HMC and NUTS, but we never
assumed those would be the final word in sampling!

We've talked about adding auto-dif for Hessians, but
the main drawback's scalability.

 > world, there is a standard set of test problems, but I haven't seen a similar set for MCMC methods -

We implemented and tested almost all of the BUGS
models, which are a kind of MCMC de facto test
standard.

> might be a useful exercise to generate a standard set so the community can properly evaluate different approaches.
>
> Not very exciting work, but extremely valuable, and IMHO a necessary condition for a mature technology.

We completely agree.  Building out the model set is one of
the deliverables for our NSF grant for Stan, so we plan to
do much more of it beyond the basic BUGS models.  There are
entire textbooks devoted to BUGS examples that we can port.

We're mostly focused on practical statistical models we
care about involving multilevel regressions, particularly
ones requiring multivariate priors.

I also think it helps to have toy test problems like the Rosenbrock
to understand the theoretical properties of an algorithm.

Other simple cases to look at in addition to banana-shaped
densities like the Rosenbrock are thin and thick tails, as
well as the funnel-shaped distrbutions that approximate what
happens in some multilevel models.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
To Bob's detailed comments, I'll just add that it's interesting that
you're finding that setting epsilon too low is getting you stuck! One
scenario I can imagine that happening in is:
1. You start somewhere very very far away from where the sampler
ultimately ends up.
2. So the sampler has to get from a point with extremely high
potential energy to one with much lower potential energy.
3. Doing that with accurate simulations could require many, many
resamplings of the momenta, since you can only transform a limited
amount of potential energy into kinetic energy before the simulation
gets inaccurate.
4. So NUTS drives the step size ever downward while warming up,
eventually hitting the maximum number of iterations, even though using
an inaccurate simulation would be fine for the earliest "search" phase
of warmup.
Do you think that's what's happening here? This phenomenon does seem
to argue for using some kind of more intelligent initial
optimization-based search phase to initialize the sampler. Could be a
nice application for a general-purpose black-box variational inference
algorithm like the one by Gershman et al. (2012; and I'm not just
saying that because I'm the second author!).

Matt

Hi Nigel,

This is absolutely worth thinking about. In fact, I'd say that the
LBFGS-HMC method of Zhang and Sutton is doing something quite similar,
although it's inspired from a different direction.

One point to note about using the (approximate) Hessian in the
sampler—it's not valid to let the Hessian change from iteration to
iteration unless you're very careful (as in Girolami and Calderhead's
RM-HMC or Zhang and Sutton's LBFGS-HMC). This is potentially a big
issue for a nasty distribution like the exponentiated Rosenbrock
function, where the local curvature information shows substantial
local variation.

messages.body_plain:
Hmmm...apples and oranges....

I was using NUTS with a single chain starting at the origin.

The Rosenbrock minimum is at (1,1,1,...). The values at my starting point is D (dimension).

I was using DREAM with multiple chains based on a Latin Hypercube (LHC) design. Initial function was much higher.

Yes indeed. It's all about the no free lunch, no one method will solve all problems efficiently.

In my optimisation work (all unpublished, it is commercially confidential), I have integrated methods from particle swarm (PSO), differential evolution (DE) and local quasi newton minimisation. It is fully integrated, not just switching from one to the other at certain iterations. These different methods all contribute usefully.

Similarly, I see HMCMC methods as being good for local search, whereas more heuristic methods like DREAM are better for global exploration.

I did start looking at whether ideas of quantum tunneling could be used with HMCMC, to go through barriers, but didn't get very far. Parallel tempering with HMCMC was, in my initial studies, too costly, but I have often thought of having one chain as HMCMC and other chains as parallel tempered DREAM.

For multi mode problems, there may be a need for multiple tunings of NUTS.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Rosenbrock test function with NUTS
messages.body_plain:
I came across a paper in a recent evolutionary computing journal by Kok and Sandrock

'Locating and characterizing the stationary points of the extended Rosenbrock function'

which explains the problem quite well. It is easy to get stuck at saddle points, and the authors found that simple random walk MCMC got stuck easily.

They got better results with particle swarm, and I got better results with DE.

Whatever, you need to jolt the system away from saddle points, and it seems most saddle points only have one negative eigenvalue for the hessian, so you have to kick (that is a technical term, OK?) in the right direction.

I can't see why an approximate hessian which had a small positive eigenvalue to make it positive definite could not, in a HMCMC scheme, give a suitable kick in approximately the right direction.

In contrast, a diagonal weight matrix would stay stuck.

Also, a hessian approximation which was not reflective of the saddle point would not help either.

DE helps because it can project over the saddle point. Similarly particle swarm (which behaves under certain conditions like a spring) will oscillate over the saddle point. Like pushing a swing and the child goes flying over the fence.

messages.subject: numerical stability issues
messages.body_plain:
On 9/3/12 8:04 AM, goodwin wrote:

> I have done a lot of work developing methods will will handle very small values on normal distributions, and very fast
> approximate schemes for cum norms. Languages like R too easily set these things to zero at extremes, and then you can't
> escape. My approximations are very happy being 1000 sd's from the mean. These things are very important for robust code.
> My actual problem has a starting point of log likelihood of minus many thousands.

> Maybe something to think about for Stan if you haven't already, but you are already generally dealing with logs.

Really low log probabilities aren't a problem.

> Simple example -
> pnorm(-1000, log.p = TRUE)
> is OK in R, but
> 1.0 - pnorm(1000, log.p = TRUE)
> returns one so you have to use the tail instead of the head.

Right.  We use the usual C++ log1p() functions with
first or second-order Taylor approximations for
values of x close to zero in log1p(x) = log(1 + x).

But I'm sure we have problems in places where we
haven't thought through all the algebra and recoded
things that look like log(1 + x) as log1p(x).

> But sometimes I want the area under the cum at tails, and then I need
> pnorm(-1000) - pnorm(-1001)
> so then you need to do some tricks.

This kind of thing could be a problem for us in truncated
models where we have to compute log diffs.   But then
if you're that far out on a truncation/censoring model,
underflow's probably the least of our concerns.

We've calculated log sums of exponents in the usual way
in cases we've come across or are part of built-in
operations.  But we haven't been too careful with the
truncated distributions involve the cumulative distribution
functions yet.

> I don't know how robust your C libraries are to these things. When these problems occur, you don't see any obvious
> manifestation.

That depends on what is happening.  If we wind up
underflowing to zero for a parameter that has to be
positive, we'll trap the domain errors, throw it, and
the sampler can report it.  Or we'll let it go and do
the right thing in the technically undefined limits.

At least that's the theory.  I'm sure we still have a long
way to go.  Hopefully the users will help us out with bug
reports.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: Problem with truncated data model [+ log CDF?]
messages.subject_clean: Problem with truncated data model [+ log CDF?]
messages.body_plain:
Good call.  Totally my bad.  And it affects all of
the truncated distributions, not just the upper-bound
only.  None of these will work properly until we release
a patched version of Stan (and RStan), which we will do ASAP.

I just pushed a patch to our code repository that
fixes the issue, which is in stan/gm/generator.hpp,
starting on line 1024 or so.

We should set up a model test as the generator isn't
tested otherwise.

I forgot the negation due to the CDF terms being in
the denominator under a log.

An upper-truncated sampling statement

    y ~ foo(...) T[,U];

should translate to the C++:

    lp__ += foo_log(y,...);
    lp__ -= log(foo_cdf(U,...));

Because I inadvertently made the second line here += instead
of -= in the generator, we'll need to test this
through a model.

The other two cases we have are with just a lower
bound, using log1m(x) == log(1 - x), to set

    "" T[L,]
    lp__ -= log1m(foo_cdf(L,...));

and with both an upper and lower bound,

    "" T[L,U]
    lp__ -= log(foo_cdf(U,...) - foo_cdf(L,...));

An earlier thread brings up the issue of whether we
should try to be more careful about underflow of the CDF
to 0 or overflow to 1.  We could definitely be much
more careful with the arithmetical precision here.

We could really use three compound log-difference CDF
functions for these three cases.

We could then test if the lower bound was less than
the upper bound, something we're currently not doing.
As is, if they're backwards, you'll try to take the log
of a negative number and get an error that way.

- Bob

On 9/4/12 10:40 AM, Nigel/essence wrote:
> Never take the log of a normal. The normal can get very small and be set to zero and/or underflow.

Absolutely.

In practice, overflow or underflow in the truncated
distributions shouldn't be much cause for concern.  There we have
terms

   -log(U - L)
   -log(1 - L)
   -log(U - 0)

where U and L are the cdf values of the upper and lower
bounds.  If these overflow to 1 or underflow to 0, there's
not much harm done :-)

The one area where it could matter is if an upper bound
underflowed or a lower-bound overflowed.  That would mean
you have a very very narrow interveral for the constraint.

> Use a specialised algorithm to get log normals.

We already do that for the probability functions and
many other functions.

As I mentioned last time, the frustrating part is that
even if the basic functions are OK, their interactions
can get messy.  For instance, we added a log Bernoulli
distribution function that took logit-scaled parameters
because applying inv_logit would underflow or overflow
to 0 or 1 in some cases with initial parameters and lead
to overall 0 probability.  (We truncated that to make
sure it didn't happen, but that's a hack, though one
Andrew's written about before under the heading 'Pinocchio
principle') -- a truncated inv_logit that's bounded between
(.01, .99) effectively handles overflow not only of the
arithmetic (for which (1E-15,1-1E-15) suffices.

> [forgive me if I am preaching to the converted]

I like listening to a good sermon on arithmetic
accuracy :-)  And thanks for the reference.  I'll read
it tonight.

- Bob

messages.subject: turning off Eigen debug
messages.body_plain:
Turning off debug isn't as straightforward as
I'd hoped.  There are two options.

Option 1:  put flags in the makefile that make
it easy to turn off all range checking in
Stan and in Eigen.

Pros:  gets rid of computation
Cons:  will seg fault instead of report errors
        won't help with models in Stan language

If that's all people want, no problem.

It's hard to control through the modeling language
because it would require recompiling the library
libstan.a with different compiler flags.

Option 2:  we could more subtly try to control
the range checks in the modeling language and Eigen.

First, do no harm.  Wherever possible, we want to avoid
the possibility of seg faults percolating through to
R and crashing it.

The current code is redundant for indexing.
Stan checks std::vector, Eigen vector, row vector
and matrix indexings generated from the modeling language.
Eigen also checks all Eigen vector, row vector and
matrix indexing and raises an indexing exception if
it finds one rather than seg faulting.

If Eigen's literally just doing assert() in the code,
I don't know that that's much better, and we probably
need to add a bunch of range checks on Eigen operations
to be safe.

Nothing in Stan checks that matrices are compatible
sizes before multiplying.  I'm not sure if Eigen does
that in the same way it checks indexing.

The doc for EIGEN_NO_DEBUG says it turns
off all asserts at both compile and run time:

   http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/TopicPreprocessorDirectives.html

Controlling our own checks one way or the other is no
problem.

- Bob

 >

Thanks for the clarification.  If it didn't work
as you just pointed out, we'd never be able to
do censored or truncated models!

Daniel and I are in the middle of debugging this
and having some problems getting simple truncated
estimates right.  The only problem is we're out of
things to test -- the model's getting translated
properly, all the gradients for the normal density
and CDF seem right, too.

I wrote a model that includes the censored
data:

data {
   real U;
   int<lower=0> N_censored;
   int<lower=0> N_observed;
   real<upper=U> y[N_observed];
}
transformed data {
   real<lower=0> sigma;
   sigma <- 1.0;
}
parameters {
   real mu;
}
model {
   for (n in 1:N_observed)

     y[n] ~ normal(mu,sigma) T[,U];

   lp__ <- lp__ + N_censored * log(1 - normal_p(U,mu,sigma));
}

I know that we should have better arithmetic precision
in all this, but I don't think that's the issue here.

I then generate 1000 training points and censor at 0 roughly
the same way as the original poster did.

 > N = 1000
 > y_raw = rnorm(N,0,1)
 > y <- y_raw[y_raw < 0]
 > U = 0
 > N_observed = length(y)
 > N_censored = N - N_observed
 > dump(c("N_observed","N_censored","y","U"))

With all this in place, we're getting estimates of
mu around 1.0.  And often very ill-behaved adaptation
(massive step sizes).

If I take the line for censored data out of the model,
everything works about how you'd expect (a slight
underestimate of the true mean used to generate the data).
So it seems like it must be a problem with normal_p.

But all the tests for normal_p show all systems go.

I had to add in a signature declaration for normal_p in
stan/gm to get it to run.

- Bob

The problem is that I never put any index
checks on the left hand side of assignments.

The left-hand-side of an assignment is treated
separately from general expression indexing
because the syntax for lvalues is limited.

So I'm afraid the answer is yes, I do want to put
those checks in.  So the compiled code would
look similar to what it looks like for the
get_base1() calls in the code now.

   for (unsigned int i = 1; i < K; i++) {
     check_range(vector,i,"v");
     v[i-1] = ...;
   }

and we'd have a support function like:

   template <typename T>
   inline check_range(const std::vector<T>& x,
                      size_t i,
                      const char* msg) {
   #if (!defined NDEBUG) || (!defined STAN_NO_DEBUG)
       if (i < 1 || i > x.size())
           ... throw some kind of idx exception ...
   #endif
   }

We need to make sure check_range is included as a header
so it can get compiled with the right flags.

messages.subject: branches, versions, and maintenance
messages.body_plain:
Ben brought up the issue of branching
our code and what goes into which branch:

   We also probably need a branch called v1.0.x or v1.x. And a set of
   guidelines for what goes in what branch. And to write down our
   accumulated set of guidelines so that other people can find them.

Below is what I think.  Anyone else have an opinion?

Given our limited resources, my thinking was that we would
NOT support anything other than the currently distributed
version.  That means we tag the releases for laughs, but
don't maintain them going forward.

In particular, I want to respond to users who say they're
using an old version by first telling them to upgrade,
then report bugs.

I don't even care if we distribute older versions.  We
can leave them on Google Code and deprecate them, but I
don't want people following links to older versions when
newer versions are available.

Within minor versions, when going from 1.x.y to 1.x.(y+1),
there's no reason to support 1.x.y going forward.

It's more of an issue when we change functionality, as in
going from 1.0.y to 1.1.0.  But as long as we don't break
backward compatibility, there shouldn't be a problem for users
in supporting just the newer versions.

When we change major versions AND they break backward
compatibility, say going from 1.1.x to 2.0.0, it may be
worth taking up this discussion again.

For commercial customers, things are different.  They often
don't want to upgrade even minor versions of software that
works as it is.  Or they weren't sold a license that lets
them upgrade.  Given that we're not selling Stan, I don't
see that as an issue, either.

What bigger companies do for commercial software (e.g.,
MS for Windows or Office, Oracle for Java) is support some older
versions, then eventually retire them so that support doesn't
drag on forever.  Apple's very agressive at retiring old version
support compared to MS.

- Bob

(at least in the sense of not being buggy) and have
made a few patches elsewhere for error checking, I'd like

I'll get the Stan 1.0.1 release ready to go by tomorrow
afternoon at the latest.  Hopefully Jiqiang can plug it
into RStan 1.0.1 tomorrow or Friday and we can release
1.0.1 on Friday.

I'm happy there are so few bugs being reported.  (I'm
less happy at the trouble people are having with the
variable declarations and order dependency.)

messages.subject: Fwd: HMC Diagnostics
messages.body_plain:
I thought other people might benefit from this, too.
It's going to take a bit of work to build some of
these into Stan, but they should all be possible.

- Bob

 From Michael Betancourt:
------------------
Below is a list of the diagnostics I have at the ready for when my chains don't behave as expected.  I'm ignoring the
gradient/Hessian checks, as well as the checks of the metric implementation when using RMHMC.

verboseEvolve:
   Evolve the current state by one half momentum step, one full position step, and then one half momentum step,
displaying H, and ( \Delta H / epsilon^{2} ) at each update.  The idea is that if the leapfrog is working properly then
you should see the cancellation of errors (some error in one direction, then lots of error in the other direction, then
error in the first direction again to cancel the bulk of the difference).

checkIntError:
   Evolve the current state by a given number of iterations, displaying H and ( \Delta H / epsilon^{2} ) at each update
so that you can see if the error is only slowly increasing or straight up diverging for the given evolution parameters.

saveTrajectory:
     Evolve the current state through a single trajectory, saving each update to a file.  This way you can plot the
entire trajectory and check it visually for problems (helpful in diagnosing divergences, bad step-sizes, etc).

plotSamples:
     Save the proposed sample, proposed potential, and acceptance probability in the chain, then display the visual
diagnostics we've discussed before, namely histograms of each marginal distribution for samples with p(accept) < 0.1 and
p(accept) > 0.9.  For NUTS you'd have to play around with this a bit -- Matt had recommended looking at the average
acceptance probability across the entire chain, but I'm not sure which sample you'd plot in that case.  You'd do just as
well plotting each step along the trajectory along with what its acceptance probability would be, provided the storage
of all those samples doesn't cause issues.
---------------------

messages.subject: Re: branches, versions, and maintenance
messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, September 5, 2012 5:10:08 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Given our limited resources, my thinking was that we would
> NOT support anything other than the currently distributed
> version.  That means we tag the releases for laughs, but
> don't maintain them going forward.

I agree that our preference is for users to upgrade to the latest version. But having tagged old releases serves at least two additional purposes. One is to serve as endpoints for a git bisect when something that was previously working is later found to be broken and we don't know why. You can do

git bisect start HEAD v1.2 --      # HEAD is bad, v1.2 is good

to find the commit that caused the problem. This works best when the tag for the working state is recent.

Also, some projects prefer that people branch off the last released version rather than whatever state master is in

git branch feature v1.2

This can make it easier to merge those branches into master later.

> It's more of an issue when we change functionality, as in
> going from 1.0.y to 1.1.0.  But as long as we don't break
> backward compatibility, there shouldn't be a problem for users
> in supporting just the newer versions.
>
> When we change major versions AND they break backward
> compatibility, say going from 1.1.x to 2.0.0, it may be
> worth taking up this discussion again.

We also need a policy as to what the process should be for deciding whether something that goes into master also goes into 1.1.0 and / or 1.0.y . For a lot of projects, the "release manager" is asked on the list to git cherry-pick commit deadbeef from master to whatever branch is waiting to be released. In other projects, people git cherry-pick commit deadbeef to whatever branch they personally feel is appropriate and announce it on the list to see if there are any objections. But we probably don't want to be in a situation where the release manager doesn't know what is going into the release he is managing.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] branches, versions, and maintenance
messages.body_plain:
In short, I'm a plus one for what Bob said. Some comments below.

On Wed, Sep 5, 2012 at 5:10 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> Ben brought up the issue of branching
> our code and what goes into which branch:
>
>   We also probably need a branch called v1.0.x or v1.x. And a set of
>   guidelines for what goes in what branch. And to write down our
>   accumulated set of guidelines so that other people can find them.
>
> Below is what I think.  Anyone else have an opinion?
>
> Given our limited resources, my thinking was that we would
> NOT support anything other than the currently distributed
> version.  That means we tag the releases for laughs, but
> don't maintain them going forward.
>
> In particular, I want to respond to users who say they're
> using an old version by first telling them to upgrade,
> then report bugs.
>
> I don't even care if we distribute older versions.  We
> can leave them on Google Code and deprecate them, but I
> don't want people following links to older versions when
> newer versions are available.

Agreed. We can just be diligent about keeping our current downloads
up-to-date. And we'll leave the tagged versions in our repository.

> Within minor versions, when going from 1.x.y to 1.x.(y+1),
> there's no reason to support 1.x.y going forward.
>
> It's more of an issue when we change functionality, as in
> going from 1.0.y to 1.1.0.  But as long as we don't break
> backward compatibility, there shouldn't be a problem for users
> in supporting just the newer versions.
>
> When we change major versions AND they break backward
> compatibility, say going from 1.1.x to 2.0.0, it may be
> worth taking up this discussion again.

Ben was suggesting we define what goes into each branch. As a
proposal, how is this for a start?
- Major version: additional functionality (major, whatever that
means), no guarantee on backwards compatibility
- Minor version: additional functionality (minor), backwards compatible
- Patch version: bug fixes, backwards compatible, might include
additional functionality

I would think adding new samplers would increase minor version. Maybe
NUTS3 would increase major version or not. Solving MCMC definitely
increases the major version. Maybe twice. Fixing numeric stability
increases patch version.

> For commercial customers, things are different.  They often
> don't want to upgrade even minor versions of software that
> works as it is.  Or they weren't sold a license that lets
> them upgrade.  Given that we're not selling Stan, I don't
> see that as an issue, either.
>
> What bigger companies do for commercial software (e.g.,
> MS for Windows or Office, Oracle for Java) is support some older
> versions, then eventually retire them so that support doesn't
> drag on forever.  Apple's very agressive at retiring old version
> support compared to MS.

I also think this is a non-issue. If a later version fixes the problem
and a user (commercial or non) doesn't want to download a newer
version, I don't think we should prioritize our efforts making fixes
to older versions. If someone volunteers to maintain older versions, I
won't stop them.

messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, September 5, 2012 7:38:15 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Now that I have, I completely agree.  I would
> think branching on major versions makes sense.
>
> I don't know how to do it in git, though.

git branch takes an optional start-point, which can be a tag or a hash but defaults to HEAD.

> > One is to serve as endpoints for a git bisect when something that was previously working
> > is later found to be broken and we don't know why. You can do
> >
> > git bisect start HEAD v1.2 --      # HEAD is bad, v1.2 is good
> >
> > to find the commit that caused the problem. This works best when the tag for the working state is recent.
>
> That sounds like a great idea.  Can you not
> do it commit by commit?

Doing it one commit at a time would be unefficient. Under a bisection algorithm,

git bisect start HEAD v1.2 --

git bisect good # 1
git bisect bad  #  2
git bisect bad  #  3
...
git bisect good # K

you get approximately halfway to the bad commit at each of the K steps.

> > We also need a policy as to what the process should be for deciding whether something that goes into master also goes
> > into 1.1.0 and / or 1.0.y .
>
> I'd rather not push backwards.  What's the benefit
> of doing that?

Presuming that everything that goes into 1.1.0 or 1.0.y will also go into master (and thus 2.0.0), then you always have to commit to multiple places. Given that, every project that I know of commits to master first so that anyone can git pull origin/master and see the commit(s). And then there is some process by which it is decided whether to also commit it to 1.1.0 or 1.0.y .

>  > For a lot of projects, the "release manager" is asked on the list to git cherry-pick commit
> > deadbeef from master to whatever branch is waiting to be released. In other projects, people git cherry-pick commit
> > deadbeef to whatever branch they personally feel is appropriate and announce it on the list to see if there are any
> > objections. But we probably don't want to be in a situation where the release manager doesn't know what is going into
> > the release he is managing.
>
> Let me digest that (sorry). But first, what's "deadbeef"?

8 symbols of a hypothetical SHA-1 hash. As in "Should we put commit 'deadbeef' into the 1.1.0 branch?"

> I'm happy to read external things if there is some
> kind of best practices doc going over this kind of
> thing.

There are different ways of doing everything. Here is a nice blogpost

https://rwmj.wordpress.com/2010/05/14/git-cherry-pick-wins/

Ben

messages.subject: assigning data array/vec/matrix to param array/vec/matrixe
messages.subject_clean: assigning data array/vec/matrix to param array/vec/matrixe
messages.body_plain:
As is, Stan doesn't support assignment of DATA matrices,
vectors, arrays, to PARAMETER matrices, vectors, arrays.
The issue Daniel found is that the parser accepts it, but
C++ won't compile the result.

Because we want everything that's parsable by Stanc to
be compilable by C++, this has to be fixed.  I outline the
problem and suggest two fixes below.  Any opinions?

The instances that are problematic are:

   { transformed param var,
     local var in transformed param,
     local var in model }
   <-
   { data var,
     transformed data var,
     constant* }

* We don't actually have any non-scalar constants, but if we
did, they would pose a problem.

There are no parameters in scope when the transformed
data block runs, so the reverse assignment, which is also
legal in C++, never comes up in Stan.

Fix 1.  Disallow the assignment in the parser and
add a description to the doc.

I'm OK with this fix, but it's going to be a bit
complex to implement.  I think I'll have to either
(a) propagate var/non-var info along with other type
info in Stan type inference, or (b) walk down the
expression tree corresponding to the right-hand-side
of expressions looking for variables.

Fix 2.  Wrap the constant in an auto-dif variable.

This is OK semantically.  And it's the easiest to
implement.  It shouldn't affect efficiency of param to param
assignment because I'll just wrap the right-hand-side of
assignments to transformed parameters and local
vars in transformed parameters and the model block with
a to_var() the way we do in the matrix lib.

I'm inclined to go with this option, letting the user
write inefficient models rather than having them struggle
with inscrutable edge conditions of the assignment syntax.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
So to be clear, the issue is that:

data {
  matrix[4,5] A;
  matrix[4,5] B;
}

model {
  matrix[4,5] C;
  C <- A - B;
}

will parse fine but won't compile?  Also, I assume this is specific to
matrix/vector/array types because I'm sure C[i,j] <- 1.0 would work.
The underlying issue being that the compiler doesn't know how to
convert from, e.g., Eigen::Matrix<double> to Eigen::Matrix<var>.

At any rate, I vote for fix 2.  Fix 1 would create an annoying corner
case for people to deal with if we made it illegal.  My only concern
is the performance hit, but it should be basically free when it's not
necessary.

Cheers,
Marcus

Just to say I have patched rstan somehow that I do not have the problem described below though I have not figure out what is the real reason for one issue.  So I think I am ready for the release.

There are two problems.

1. weird segfault I talked before. It is not a problem with the memory on my computer.  It is just because if the dynamic shared object is released by R's garbage collector earlier than the c++ object that is exposed by Rcpp, we would have segfault when R is releasing the c++ object (but the compiled code is gone).  Normally this would happen since the dynamic object is unloaded later.

2. previously it seems that compiling two different stan model is problematic as the later will overwrite the first one.  I have not figure out why.  But now I use different Rcpp module names for different models, which seems to be able to _control_ the problem.

--
Jiqiang

messages.subject: remove useless matrix minus() functions?
messages.body_plain:
I figured out why Daniel and I were talking
at cross purposes.  Someone (maybe even me in a past life),
added functions to stan/agrad/matrix with signatures:

   template <typename T>
   inline var minus(const T& v);

   template <typename T>
   inline vector_v minus(const Eigen::Matrix<T, Eigen::Dynamic, 1>& v);

   template <typename T>
   inline row_vector_v minus(const Eigen::Matrix<T, 1, Eigen::Dynamic>& rv);

Unless anyone objects, I'm going to delete these.

If T is an agrad var, the more specific functions
with Matrix<var,...> types will be called.
If T is double, the more specific functions with
Matrix<double,...> will be called.

The one issue where it would be a problem would be if
T were float or int or something, which can't happen
in Stan model generated code, but could in C++.  But
even if T were float, you wouldn't want to do this kind
of auto-promotion from double to var.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the reference I will check it out.

Some arm waving:

- with multiple chains, different chains can use different samplers.

- there needs to be some way of cross fertilising between different chains, e.g. as in parallel tempering, or using 'other' chains to generate Hessians.

- different samplers have different overheads/function evaluations per sample. You can have some chains heavy duty, some chains light duty.

- you don't necessarily have to integrate different techniques into a single sampler, different techniques can be spread across different chains.

- adapting more than one parameter in a chain (epsilon plus something else) starts to get tricky and can easily become unstable. I tried once to adapt temperatures and epsilon in a single tempered scheme, and it was a disaster.

Concerning Hessians:

- there are (at least) two distinct problems.

- One is how to move between different modes. In this case, too much forcing of positive definiteness can hinder such moves in a Hamiltonian scheme. When at a saddle point, we want to move across the saddle point to another mode, so we want a Hessian with a suitable very small positive eigenvalue in that direction. But it can remain very difficult to get up to the saddle point in the first place, so some scheme which allows the Hessian to be ill conditioned and do long steps is perversely useful.

- I'm not sure how it works to have negative weights .... I once had a student friend at Cambridge who did a PhD in what happens to the laws of physics if you go faster than the speed of light, and he never recovered his sanity.

- Another is how to sample efficiently within a mode. In this case a good Hessian can be useful, but we don't want it contaminated by information from chains which are in some different mode.

- It is almost as if we want both a local positive definite Hessian and a long range ill conditioned Hessian.

- this is similar to proxy modelling which has a linear regression component which models long range effects, and a more local radial basis function component to ensure interpolation.

- As we know, defining Hessian approximations which preserve balance etc. are tricky.

- maybe stochastic techniques such as CMAES could be useful - I have tried and rejected this well known method for optimisation simply because I didn't like the way it handled simple bound constraints.

In short, BFGS or other Hessian schemes which have only been tested on relatively simple single mode problems are probably going to demonstrate some shortcomings i more complex problems, which their proponents already acknowledge. The background of these methods is in local optimisation, not global optimisation.

The splitting papers referred to above have a lot of examples of application to multi mode problems.

messages.body_plain:
> - One is how to move between different modes. In this case, too much forcing of positive definiteness can hinder such moves in a Hamiltonian scheme. When at a saddle point, we want to move across the saddle point to another mode, so we want a Hessian with a suitable very small positive eigenvalue in that direction. But it can remain very difficult to get up to the saddle point in the first place, so some scheme which allows the Hessian to be ill conditioned and do long steps is perversely useful.

There are two issues here: Hamiltonian evolution and MCMC.

Indefinite metrics are a problem for Hamiltonian evolution because the
trajectories will never be able to cross the boundary where the metric
changes signature.  (Remember the log determinant term!  If the metric
changes signature smoothly then there has to be a point where one of
the eigenvalues is zero, hence the determinant vanishes, - log |
\Lambda | = \infty, and an infinite potential wall appears between the
regions of varying signature.  The resulting joint distribution for
(p, q) is reducible and your chain is no longer ergodic).  Not only do
indefinite metrics not help transition between regions of opposite
curvature they isolate them exactly!

On the MCMC side, If the metric is not positive definite (e.g. Hessian
outside of a convex support) then the conditional distribution for the
momenta is not a Gaussian and the Gibbs iterations don't make sense
anymore.

It's called "Riemannian manifold" HMC for a reason.  Lorentzian
signature'd metrics mess up the MCMC side, and even if you could get
past that you'd have to worry about problems with Hamiltonian
evolution (really you want to move to a Poisson manifold, but those
things are crazy weird and I don't think anyone knows how to
simulation flow on them.)

Just a word of caution on multimodal problems: no method can handle
the general case. In general, finding the global maximum of (say) a
continuously differentiable objective function f simply cannot be done
with finite computation. Sampling from exp(f) is a harder problem than
finding the maximum of f, which means that in the general case
sampling is harder than impossible.

That's not to say that we shouldn't pay attention to multimodal
problems. But it's probably best to temper one's expectations when
thinking about methods that promise to solve global optimization.
(Sorry for the pun.)

Matt

messages.body_plain:
You're right, you can't just scramble everything post-hoc when
computing ESS. The reason is a little subtle—the identity underlying
the ESS calculation assumes a stationary process, and the process "run
a Markov chain for N iterations and then scramble the result" is not
stationary (it only happens once). But as long as you're working with
a stationary process all is well. You basically just have to think of
the multiple interacting chains as one big Markov chain whose state
consists of a number of vectors each of whose marginal stationary
distributions is the target distribution.

Matt

>>>>
>>>> as not mixing well.
>>>>
>>>>
>>>
>>> ps. but with suitable swapping, all the chains can mix nicely?
>>
>>
>> They would, but then the convergence diagnostics (Rhat at the very
>> least) are no longer applicable because the chains are not
>> independent.  It's a non-trivial question to derive a convergence
>> diagnostic that can properly handle multiple, interacting chains.  In
>> the worst case, you can try to treat all chains as a single chain and
>> use the single chain diagnostics, but that is decidedly
>> unsatisfying...
>
>
> We were discussing this issue at the Stan meeting last week
> w.r.t. DE/DREAM/ensemble sampling.  These samplers evolve
> a bunch of parallel particles consisting of multiple copies of
> the parameters, which together form a Markov chain.  But
> each copy of a parameter has some dependence on the other copies
> introduced by the differential evolution (ensemble sampling).
>
> If I understood Matt properly, he was saying the ESS calcs still work even
> if you just concatenate a bunch of unrelated Markov chains.
> I still don't follow, because then it would also
> seem you could just scramble everything.   Goodman and Weare
> discuss the issue in their paper, but I didn't understand it.
> They're local (NYU), so I could perhaps go talk to them and figure
> out what's going on.
>
> - Bob

multimodal posteriors is incredibly hard and no one has a silver
bullet which will work well for every problem.  Stan is a great
platform on which these methods can be tested, but we can't expect
miracles.

But if an engineer has an urgent meeting to discuss whether to dispose an oil reservoir or not, and needs the uncertainty analysis from the sampling, and the full sampling takes a day to perform - they are not going to wait 2 - 4 days. An hour is about their limit.

It reminds me, going back to the multi mode issue. I had a client a few years ago, who had an oil reservoir model, and they seemed to have two different modes, one with high permeability/low porosity, and the other with low permeability/high porosity. Both modes matched historical measurements equally well. One mode gave a high future production forecast, the other had production falling rapidly. But they had to make a decision whether to divest the field or not (worth many billions of USD), and had little way of knowing whether the sampling was properly weighting the likelihoods in the two modes.

In practice, they decided to perform further measurements to distinguish the modes. Turned out the low production forecast model was the correct one.

Of course, they should have presented the 'high production forecast' model as the truth and flogged the oil field off to somebody who didn't know how to do uncertainty analysis.

Does that help explain why multi mode and complex distributions are of great interest, even though they may pose many difficulties? HMCMC makes many intractable problems possible,which is why I use it as the basis.

To put it into perspective, proper Bayesian forecasting is still in its infancy in the oil and gas reservoir engineering industry.

The same issues arise, for example, in weather forecasting models.

Got to go catch a flight to Houston from London.

But they had to make a decision whether to divest the field or not (worth many billions of USD), and had little way of knowing whether the sampling was properly weighting the likelihoods in the two modes.
>
> In practice, they decided to perform further measurements to distinguish the modes. Turned out the low production forecast model was the correct one.

Hopefully the decisions made with one-hour deadlines are
sub-billion dollar!

> Of course, they should have presented the 'high production forecast' model as the truth and flogged the oil field off to somebody who didn't know how to do uncertainty analysis.

On the model of "guns don't kill people, people kill
people", we should have "statisticians don't swindle customers,
businesspeople swindle customers".

> Does that help explain why multi mode and complex distributions are of great interest,

I think we all agree that multimodal posterior models
are of great interest.

Part of the utility of the R-hat statistic is in
diagnosing when a sampler has chains stuck in different
modes.   Or when the distribution's so complex that it's
not mixing.

In some cases, like having two known modes,
it can even be tractable to sample if you can find the
weight of each mode somehow (for instance, through
appropriate MCMC methods that can jump between modes
while preserving stationarity).

In other cases, like the kinds of models Matt and I have
spent lots of time working on (HMMs, LDA, etc.),
the posterior is so multimodal, there's truly no hope
for MCMC to draw an effective sample.  Further, some
algorithmic tricks are needed to even compute
basic expectations from HMMs.  So despite the interest,
we're not really focusing on HMM-like structured models in
Stan, either.

- Bob

On Tue, Sep 11, 2012 at 5:37 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
> On Tuesday, September 11, 2012 5:22:49 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>>
>> Multivariate normals may be a problem, though, in that
>> we won't be able to easily compute the gradients (or maybe
>> they're easier than I suspect?).
>
>
> The gradient wrt mu is not bad. The gradient wrt the primitive parameters
> underlying Sigma is more difficult, especially considering that
> multi_normal() wouldn't know how Sigma was constructed.
>

We could vectorize multi_normal_cholesky first and write the
vectorized mult_normal in terms of that.  The derivatives wrt L should
be more straight forward in the cholesky form.  Both cases would need
to rely on the identities

d inv(A) = - inv(A) * dA * inv(A)

and

d log(det(A)) = Tr(inv(A) dA)

for matrix A.  Given those both forms should be relatively straight forward.

Also, on a side note about vectorizing things.  For large N

for (i = 1:N) {
  a += foo(b[i])
}

is *much* slower than

vector[N] tmp;

for (i = 1:N) {
  tmp[i] = foo(b[i]);
}

a += sum(tmp);

This is true regardless of the complexity of foo().  The extra
allocation and assignment operations are cheap compared to the N extra
vari instantiations implied by the repeated += operations.  This is
probably not true with a is not a variable.

This applies equally well for a model or for a vectorized
implementation of a function.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Stan and RStan 1.0.1
messages.body_plain:
We are happy to announce the release of
Stan/RStan 1.0.1.  See:

   http://mc-stan.org/

1.0.1 is a patch release that fixes some major issues
with assignments to parameters, truncated probability
functions, visibility of functions within the modeling
language, and several minor issues.

The manual has also been double-checked to make
sure all of the code compiles and to incorporate all the
typo fixes people have submitted (thanks again!).

On the horizon, in addition to bug fixes, we have prioritized
vectorizing the remaining probability functions, adding more
cumulative distribution functions, adding new data types
to support multivariate analysis including constraints on
vector and matrix types, adding basic discrete sampling,
and parallelizing calls to Stan.

Please don't hesitate to contact the user's group
mailing list with questions, comments, or suggestions.

- Stan Development Team

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Rosenbrock test function with NUTS
messages.body_plain:
Not so simple.

I'm already running all my hyperthreads at 100%, but use threads calculating the function rather than using threads for the different chains. I used to use threads for chains, but sometimes you want different samplers in different chains, and the samplers have different performance characteristics, so then splitting chains between threads does not fully utilise them. Eg a DREAM thread and NUTS thread - not the best way to do it.

Fear not, I am fully multi threaded from the ground up, at an appropriate level of granularity.

Of course, how to multi thread is very much problem specific. Most people would want to have a thread/chain architecture.

But even with a thread/chain architecture, you could have 21 simple chains using 7 threads and 1 complex chain (e.g. NUTS) using 1 thread, depending on how many leadfrogs NUTS takes per step.

I have also, btw, experimented with GPU, and have done a lot of profiling and benchmarking and tuning.

For example - the cdf of a Gaussian is very expensive, so I use a good enough approximation which is very fast. Similarly, I use Matern correlation functions, but not the exact function, a good approximation is good enough.

There is a general lesson - balance out your errors! If your sampling is going to give you something +/- 2%, why are you looking for exact values of special functions?

I even do an approximation of exp.

Of course, you have to be consistent and careful your approximations are smooth and differentiable etc., and you use them consistently.

But the biggest improvements, once you have done all the tuning, is to find better algorithms.

messages.body_plain:
Getting seriously off track, but -};!} (I'm not very good at smileys).

I am not in control of the computers, I am developing an end user application. Some of the clients have access to thousands of powerful computers in a cluster, some only have a stand alone laptop.

If it was just for me, I would but a 4 socket AMD 16 core machine, you can get them for under $10K. 64 threads. I don't have time and energy to build a simple cluster myself.

I would guess that a set of completely independent runs is less efficient than a set of chains which can mix and cross fertilise.

For example, with DREAM it is definitely beneficial to have a large number of chains in a run.  2xN is recommended.

So you can't just set off independent jobs to independent computers and aggregate.

I am only writing this now because I am taking a break as one of my clients has set off 200 simulation jobs to their cluster, and the results of the engineering jobs will be complete tomorrow morning. My own software controls and manages all these simulation runs, in a multi threaded environment using a producer/consumer paradigm (Ben at least will know what that means). The jobs can take different times, so as soon as one is finished I set off another one, and each time I do a MCMC simulation.

Which reminds me - potentially one of the biggest algorithmic improvements I envisage is when I learn about how to take full advantage of previous MCMC samples when generating a new set of samples - each time, the underlying likelihood function has changed, but gradually converges. I use this fact to have an intelligent way of initiating the chains when I start the MCMC again, but could do a lot more. One obvious thing is I can avid the burn-in after the first time, or at least make it much shorter. Can I sample from the previous set of samples? I'm sure I can do a lot in this area, but not this week.

To be clear I have a workflow:

(a) construct likelihood function
(b) perform MCMC (ideally << 1 hour)
(c) perform full engineering simulation study (0.1 - 24 hours)
(d) update likelihood function
(e) perform MCMC (ideally << 10 mins)
(f) go to (c) until finished

ps one of my clients did, indeed, use their heavyweight computer cluster to do the MCMC part, but that was with a basic RW algorithm back in 2005 or so. In the dark ages.

Seriously, tell me if my input is of interest or a distraction, and I will stop writing essays. There can't be many people who are developing commercial end user applications using advanced MCMC methods, are there?

messages.subject: threads; GPU; errors and approximations
messages.body_plain:
On 9/12/12 9:54 PM, Nigel/essence wrote:

> I'm already running all my hyperthreads at 100%, but use threads calculating the function rather than using threads for the different chains. I used to use threads for chains, but sometimes you want different samplers in different chains, and the samplers have different performance characteristics, so then splitting chains between threads does not fully utilise them. Eg a DREAM thread and NUTS thread - not the best way to do it.
>
> Fear not, I am fully multi threaded from the ground up, at an appropriate level of granularity.
>
> Of course, how to multi thread is very much problem specific. Most people would want to have a thread/chain architecture.
>
> But even with a thread/chain architecture, you could have 21 simple chains using 7 threads and 1 complex chain (e.g. NUTS) using 1 thread, depending on how many leadfrogs NUTS takes per step.

Are you using the executor framework in java.util.concurrent?
I'd think you'd just queue up Runnable objects and then bound the
number of concurrent threads to not overwhelm your machine.

Unless the objects needed to communicate with each other.
Then you'd wind up with a complicated scheduling problem.

Boy, do I ever miss util.concurrent in C++!   Unfortunately,
Doug Lea wasn't happy with the new java community organization
under Oracle and opted out of participating.

I assume you're also cutting down all short-term object
allocation so one of those threads isn't just hammering away
full time on GC.  The GC's so good now that it's not even
noticeable until you start getting contention across as many
threads as you have CPUs.

Do you find using the hyperthreads helps?  I've found it
a very mixed bag.  For instance, MATLAB works better with the
number of threads set to the number of cores, not the number
of "hyper"-cores.  But it defaults to the number of hypercores.

Are you using an external matrix library in Java?  I
never found one that looked good, but I stopped looking
many years ago.

> I have also, btw, experimented with GPU, and have done a lot of profiling and benchmarking and tuning.

Specialized architectures are a tradeoff in speed
versus flexibility.  For instance, I'm pretty sure
most GPUs only support 32-bit arithmetic.

GPUs are effective if you can formulate your problem
as 32-bit single-instruction/multiple-data operations.

Everyone I've ever talked to has concluded they're
not worth the effort, but that's because I don't talk
to people who tend to need to do the same computation
every week, just really really fast.

> For example - the cdf of a Gaussian is very expensive, so I use a good enough approximation which is very fast. Similarly, I use Matern correlation functions, but not the exact function, a good approximation is good enough.
>
> There is a general lesson - balance out your errors!

Absolutely.  That's why you don't need to usually run
very many effective samples to get estimates with
fractions of the deviation of the variable you're estimating.

 > If your sampling is going to give you something +/- 2%, why are you
 > looking for exact values of special functions?

Having said that, the reason to not do approximations in
NUTS/HMC is that the leapfrog step acceptance is pretty sensitive
to such errors.

The main reason not to accept +/- 2% approximation errors (as opposed
to something like 1e-10) is that the errors can compound.

In the best situation, the errors would all cancel out -- is
that what you mean by "balance"?

- Bob

messages.subject: vectorizing with sum() vs. repeated +=
messages.body_plain:
On 9/11/12 7:10 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:

> Also, on a side note about vectorizing things.  For large N
>
> for (i = 1:N) {
>    a += foo(b[i])
> }
>
> is *much* slower than
>
> vector[N] tmp;
>
> for (i = 1:N) {
>    tmp[i] = foo(b[i]);
> }
>
> a += sum(tmp);
>

> .. The extra

> allocation and assignment operations are cheap compared to the N extra
> vari instantiations implied by the repeated += operations.  This is
> probably not true with a is not a variable.

Right -- the speed's from not allocating vari objects and
having to visit them and call their virtual functions during
derivative propagation.

I just dropped a note to that effect in the manual section
on vectorization.

I've thought about this issue before (though not so far
as to vectorize it with sum()), and I think we can
probably use an expression template for the result
of += to lazily drop a sequence of += into a vector sum.

By concentrating on +=, we wouldn't need to
do tons of overloads and conversions as we would with
a more full template expression approach.

    sum_expression& operator+=(sum_expression&, var&);

    sum_expression& operator+=(var&, var&);

and then we'd need a copy constructor for var
to create the vectorized sum:

    var(sum_expression);

> This applies equally well for a model or for a vectorized
> implementation of a function.

Exactly the same principle.

- Bob

I'm not sure that would work because the return type of operator+= is
generally ignored unless someone does (a += b) += c or d = (a += b) or
something similarly obtuse and strange.  In fact, += has to be defined
as a member function:

class var {
...
  var &operator+=(const var &b);
...
}

would need a sum vari which can have a variable size and have things
added to it.  I think this would break the rules of a vari as it's
value cannot change once its instantiated.

I think the key here is to just write smart C++ code taking this into
account.  In terms of all the "lp__ +=" operations in a model, we
could just as easily push the RHS of those statements into a vector
and then call a single sum at the end.  (I'm not sure if I've
impemented the sum vari operation to handle a vector<var> type, but
that shouldn't be too hard.

I won;t respond to every comment, mainly because we are on the sme page.

Yes, I use the latest concurrent package in Java. I played around a lot with how to reduce overhead

- callable v runnable
- how to communicate back results (e.g. using Future's)
- new inner classes or reuse existing classes
- how to allocate 1000 jobs to 8 threads using queues (do it one job at a time with a fixed length thread pool, or group it into sets of 125 or whatever)

These things can make a very big difference if your threads are at a lower level of granularity. For example, I have a common pool which is reused throughout the life of the application.

I have tested threads at very fine granularity (e.g. per row in a matrix multiplication), but generally do it at a higher level.

Unravelling loops does not help much (cf C) but it is important to keep loops simple so the Java optimiser has a chance.

Java is very fast, but as far as I know is still restricted because the JVM cannot take advantage of vector processing on Intel chips. To be honest, it is difficult to find definitive answers about this - but I think I am correct. It would be so nice if the JVM was intelligent enough to be truly portable across different CPU's with different vector processing capabilities.

Bottom line is that java threads have little overhead IF AND ONLY IF you do it right. They can have a very big overhead if you do it according to some template or tutorial you find on the web. The only thing to do is to try ten different ways and benchmark. Also be very wary of profiling tools, they can seriously mislead. There is some very low level locking code which is normally very fast, but becomes a bottleneck as soon as you try to profile.

Some managers in oil and gas don't want to even hear the word probability or statistics. But it is changing.

Hardware for major oil companies moves slowly. They are sometimes a generation behind in operating systems (eg running Windows XP today).

On another topic you asked...

Yes, I write all my own matrix arithmetic. I only ever use (up to now) symmetric positive definite matrices.

I did a lot of benchmarking to find the fastest approach.

I likewise rejected all available Java matrix packages I could find. None of them deal with a symmetric matrix as a row (or column) ordered single array. Hopeless.

I translated L-BFGS-B from Fortran to Java, and so had to translate a little  Fortran LAPACK (or it may be Linpack) from Fortran to Java, but those were the easy bits to translate.

I also do a lot of tricks with things like B*V-1*BT - I don't do any matrix multiplications, I construct U-1 * BT, and then construct the uppper triangular result matrix from that. The result is then, of course, factorised again.

Obvious tricks, but worth the effort, they can double speed.

[ B is a matrix, V-1 is the inverse of a positive definite matrix V, for which I have the cholesky factor U. ]

By default my number of threads is the number of hyperthreads. My threads tend to be small, which probably helps. My CPU is certainly showing 100% utilisation.

Memory bandwidth tends to become the bottleneck.

Unless I put my i7 Toshiba laptop under a couple of coffee mugs to aid cooling, I find that my MCMC calculations cause overheating 99% of the way through and I loose everything.

I had a similar problem a few years back with a Pentium laptop in Rio working for Petrobras, my laptop got even hotter than the friendly natives and used to crash. Must make sure I get some tickets for the next Olympics. I never got to go to any London event even though my home is London. The two tickets I got went to my sons. messages.subject: cdf, ccdf, log scale, and truncation patterns
messages.subject_clean: cdf, ccdf, log scale, and truncation patterns
messages.body_plain:
What are we going to implement for the CDFs?

Just literally implementing the cdfs is dangerous
in terms of numerical precision.

I see four functions that make sense on their own:

   foo_cdf(y,...)

   foo_cdf_log(y,...)  = log(foo_cdf(y,...))

   foo_ccdf(y,...)     = 1 - foo_cdf(y,...)

   foo_ccdf_log(y,...) = log(1 - foo_cdf(y,...))

There are numerical stability issues with trying
to calculate the log values directly or calculate
a ccdf by subtracting a cdf.

In truncated distributions, we also need to evaluate
distributions bounded above and below in (L,U) with

   foo_truncate_lu(U,L,...) = - log(foo_cdf(U,...) - foo_cdf(L,...))

                            = - log_sum_exp(foo_cdf_log(U,...),
                                            0,
                                            foo_ccdf_log(L,...))

The one-sided bounds both reduce to one of the above.
To bound above by U,

   foo_truncate_u(U,...) = - log(foo_cdf(U,...) - 0)

                         = - foo_cdf_log(U,...)

and to bound below by L,

   foo_truncate_l(L,...) = - log(1 - foo_cdf(L,...))

                         = - foo_ccdf_log(L,...)

Of course, we also need gradients of all these functions,
which means either calculating them directly or implementing
in terms of functions that can be auto-diffed.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Here are some results for Rosenbrock. 64 dimensions.

I do the integration:

INTEGRATE[R exp(-R)]

i.e. my log likelihood is rosenbrock, and I am integration a function rosenbrock.

I don't think this has any analytical solution - if anybody can suggest an integration of the form:

INTEGRATE[f exp(-R)]

as a test case, I would be very grateful...

My results are below. As I say, much less clear situation. The amount of burn-in is clearly important, and the use of BFGS is less productive. This is easy to understand in such a complex multi modal situation. i do not use a changing Hessian during leapfrogs a la Riemann paper.

Both NUTS and NUTS+DREAM+BFGS settle on a mean of about 34 - 40, but a wider range in variance of about 40 - 80. Of course, there is a danger that all the methods get stuck in a local minimum and report a variance which is too small.

My starting points are normally distributed, mean zero variance one.

In my 'real' problem I would start off with much better starting values, using different methods. I am sure that problem with a long burn-in being needed is because of poor starting points, but I am trying to expose rather than hide problems.

messages.subject: print statements for Stan
messages.body_plain:
There have been lots of user issues with initialization,
order, and NaN values creeping in.  So I'd like to
add a simple print mechanism to the models.  But I'd
like to get some feedback on my first pass on the questions
below.

Here's an example model with a print:

   parameters {
     real y;
   }
   model {
     print(y);
     y ~ normal(0,1);
   }

Every time the print statement is executed it will
print the expression text (here "y") and the expression
value (here the sampled parameter y).

(I know we've talked about printing gradients, too,
but that information isn't available as the model
is being executed.  We can add an option to the command
to print parameter gradients along with the parameters
themselves.)

I set up print() to take an arbitrary number of expressions,
so you could write print(y,mu,sigma) if you wanted.

The current output spacing is very crude because of the
way I was using carriage return (CR) but not line feed (LF)
chars in the print:

===================================
Iteration: 1990 / 2000 [ 99%]  (Sampling)
y=0.0402403:0;

y=2.08709:0;

y=0.180739:0;

y=0.614905:0;

y=-2.23667:0;

y=1.54527:0;

y=-1.60311:0;

y=0.565311:0;

y=-0.773276:0;

y=-1.44758:0;
Iteration: 2000 / 2000 [100%]  (Sampling)
y=0.277063:0;
===============================================

QUESTION:  Does anyone object to changing the CR to
CR/LF? (Technically, I'd use std::endl to get platform-specific
CR/LF behavior).  It won't look as nice for users without prints
on the command line.

QUESTION:  How many iteration numbers should we print by default?
The default is 200, with a default 2000 iterations, for a default
output of iteration number every 10 iterations.

As tempting as it is, I do NOT want to go all the way
to printf.  It's a fussy syntax we can't easily check as
the expressions are compiled, and I'd rather not induce
run-time formatting errors.

QUESTION:  Should we allow strings and skip printing the
expression by default?  For example

     print("precision_y = ", 1 / (y * y));

might print

     precision_y = 1.37828:0

(I'm afraid the :0 is for auto-dif variables and it'll
always be a 0.)

The simpler print(1 / (y * y)) proposal that I've already
implemented would print:

    (1 / (y * y)) = .277063;

I also want to point out that we can have print()
statements in transformed data (run as model is loaded),
transformed parameters (run once per leapfrog step),
and generated quantities (run once per iteration after
all leapfrog steps but before rejection step).

QUESTION:  Any other suggestions?

- Bob

Exactly!  I should've mentioned this issue.

Even if we were only doing the command-line version, it's
it's very bad practice in an API because we don't want
to control what environment our code will be run in.

Instead, what I plan to do is provide an optional ostream
pointer argument to the blocks in which the statements are
evaluated.  It'll default to 0, and the print statements
will only get called if the pointer is non-zero.

For the command line, std::cout can be passed in, and for
R, we can follow the example here:

which is more flexible than building in Rprintf() directly.
I really don't want the model code to depend on R or to have
to be generated differently by calling environment.

Along the same lines, I'm also going to need to pass in
an RNG for the generated_quantities block in order to
generate random draws from distributions.

- Bob
